justification_quote: Sec IV-B-1: "the nonlinear decision could help to amplify the subtle distinction between conflicting cues and make winner-takes-all choices [147]"; structures (Drosophila DA-GABA-MB circuit, PFC-BG-ThA-PMC, cortical column) are attributed computations by citation only ([36],[147],[150]-[161]); the paper presents no biological evidence of its own for structure-function links.

Sec IV-B-1: "the BrainCog framework is used to build Drosophila nonlinear and linear decision-making pathways as shown in Fig. 34a-b ... a two-layer SNN with LIF neurons is trained by reward-modulated STDP"; Fig 34d shows the model reproducing the nonlinear sigmoid PI curve, one setting, no control on the mapping itself.

Sec III-A: "Compared with SNNs and ANNs with the same structure that only used the BP algorithm, our model greatly improves the performance of SNNs on the DVS-CIFAR10 and DVS-Gesture datasets, while also greatly reducing the energy consumption" (Table I); Sec IV-B-2: replacing rodent with human neurons "without changing network structure can significantly improve the accuracy and completeness of an image memory task".

Abstract: "effectively validated on various supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning tasks"; instances: DVS-CIFAR10/DVS-Gesture (Table I), MNIST/Fashion-MNIST 97.9%/87.0% (Sec III-A-2), Flappy Bird and UAV decision making (Sec III-B), melody memory 99% (Sec III-D), Emotion6 (Sec III-E).

Abstract: "These brain-inspired AI models have been effectively validated on various supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning tasks, and they can be used to enable AI models to be with multiple brain-inspired cognitive functions"; Secs III-IV enumerate those validations (Table I, Fig 9, Fig 15, Fig 20).

Sec I: "Physiological studies in recent years have established a causal relationship between heterogeneous dendritic axons and the firing properties of neurons [8], neuronal heterogeneity plays an important role in determining the function of neural circuits [9]-[11] and determines the frequency of the neural spike signal [12]" — attributions carried entirely by citation; no biological evidence presented in the paper.

Sec I: TaiBai "designed from the ground up to encapsulate essential biological principles of neuronal heterogeneity, synaptic heterogeneity, flexible network topologies, and on-chip synaptic plasticity"; the mapping is instantiated by deploying diverse models on-chip (dendritic DHSNN with 4 branches, heterogeneous-neuron SRNN, on-chip learning BCI; Sec V-B-3, Fig 15), one demonstration setting per mechanism.

Sec V-C-4: "Fig. 15 includes a TaiBai-homogeneous baseline, obtained by deploying SRNN without heterogeneous neurons, DHSFNN without dendrites, and BCI cross-day decoding without on-chip learning. As can be seen from the figure, the heterogeneous neuron model makes it easier to identify the band type of ECG data, the DHSFNN with a dendritic model significantly improves the network performance, and the on-chip learning capability improves the decoding accuracy across days"; plus GPU benchmark at comparable accuracy (Fig 13(d), Fig 15).

Three task families demonstrated (ECG QTDB, speech SHD, cross-day macaque BCI; Sec V-B-3) plus standard SNN benchmarks (Fig 13(d)); scale trade-off reported once: "the number of cores increases by 4 times (182 to 749), and energy efficiency decreases by 1.7 times (6190 to 3590)" (Fig 13(e)).

Abstract: "These results demonstrated its high potentiation as a scalable, programmable, and ultra-efficient solution for both multi-scale brain simulation and brain-inspired computation" — but the evaluation covers only AI tasks (ECG, speech, BCI, SNN benchmarks); no brain-simulation experiment is presented anywhere in the paper (grep: simulation appears only in motivation and references).

Sec II: region-function attributions carried entirely by citation, e.g., "the prefrontal cortex (PFC), as its core module, is responsible for decision-making, regulating planning, execution, and task management [47]"; Brodmann [45] and HCP [46] frameworks described from literature; no biological evidence presented in the paper.

Sec I/III-A propose a mapping only: "the V1 cortical area ... is responsible for primary extraction of complex visual features, which can be implemented using CNN or YOLO [39]; ... the FPC region in the prefrontal cortex ... which we seek to emulate using LLMs"; "we simplified the corresponding functional connectivity networks, restricting interactions solely to the existing functional nodes" — no system is built or run anywhere in the paper.

Abstract: "Implementing these structures within an agent enables it to achieve basic cognitive intelligence akin to human capabilities" — the paper contains no experiment, no implementation, and no comparison; the only feasibility argument is a literature survey (Table II: "currently implemented agent architectures share similar brain-inspired structural ideas").

No demonstrated setting exists, so generality cannot be assessed; the limitations section lists open challenges ("significant limitations and challenges remain before realizing a brain-inspired agent capable of human-level intelligence") without any tested or untested task families.

Abstract claims a capability outcome ("enables it to achieve basic cognitive intelligence akin to human capabilities") while the paper presents an unimplemented proposal; Chapter IV concedes "significant limitations and challenges remain before realizing a brain-inspired agent capable of human-level intelligence" — the evidence scope is an argument by analogy plus a survey, not a demonstration.

Abstract/Sec 1: "humans have a strong generalisation ability which is beneficial from the structural and functional asymmetry of the two sides of the brain"; supported only by "converging evidence from structural and functional neuroimaging studies ... [12]" and an evolution review [13] — citation only, no biological evidence in the paper, and the asymmetry-causes-generalisation attribution itself is not evidenced.

Sec 1/3.2: "the design of dual NCP architectures replicates the human brain left and right hemispheres", with asymmetric wirings per side (Fig 3c: Left NCP 3/5 vs Right NCP 4/6); NCP itself is "inspired by C. elegans organism nervous system [16]". No evidence beyond naming that two sparse RNNs instantiate hemispheric computation; "Any instance of the LTC is essentially an RNN".

Sec 4.3: "the brain-inspired (CNN-DNCP v2) model can reduce 6.57% error when comparing with CNN model on Udacity dataset" (Fig 5.a); "The brain-inspired architecture (CNN-DNCP v4) is 5.80% and 34.05% more effective than the CNN model with regard to MSE on the cloudy and night time comma.ai recordings". The architecture grid includes single-NCP vs dual-NCP variants sharing the same CNN head (Fig 3, Sec 3.2), partially isolating the duality design; training MSE honestly reported as favouring CNN.

Generalisation tested across domains within one task family: trained on Udacity lakeside, tested on jungle; trained on comma.ai sunny, tested on cloudy/night (Sec 4.1/4.3, Fig 5) — the demonstrated gain survives several domain shifts but no other task family, scale or systematic ablation is evaluated.

Abstract: "our brain-inspired method outperforms existing methods regarding generalisation when dealing with unseen data" — evidence compares against the single reference CNN [2] plus the authors' own variants (Sec 1: "put into competition with the reference neural network mentioned in [2]"), and one variant was dropped for poor training results (Sec 4.1: "the CNN-DNCP model architecture is dropped since it takes way too long to train and the loss result is strikingly unsatisfactory").

Sec 1: brain attributions carried by citation only and acknowledged as loose: "These techniques draw loose inspiration from models of brain computations"; "Traditional NN architectures lack the concept of locality, whereas brain-inspired NN architectures prioritize it, leading to modularity ... Moreover, brain-inspired NNs tend to exhibit high sparsity" ([4],[13],[15],[16]); no biological evidence is presented.

Sec 2/3.1: stated mapping from brain principles to mechanisms: locality -> per-unit coordinates with L1 distance penalty ("A hyperparameter A, related to the network size, regulates the importance of locality"), sparsity -> Lasso penalization, modularity -> composed modules; demonstrated instantiation: the trained PINN "evolve[s] from a fully connected MLP PINN to a sparse and modular" architecture (Fig 2).

Sec 4: same-problem controlled comparisons: "The final error for the brain-inspired and fully-connected PINNs are 0.023 and 0.0094, respectively ... the brain-inspired PINN has approximately twice the error of the fully connected MLP PINN" (resource-accuracy trade-off, disclosed); "the modular PINN has a test error (calculated as MSE) that is approximately two orders lower than the fully-connected MLP PINN" (Fig 5, 3 modules of 3 units vs 9-unit MLP).

All evidence is on 1D Poisson-type equations with harmonic sources ("For demonstration purposes, this work focuses on solving the one-dimensional Poisson equation", Sec 3.1) plus a spectral-bias demonstration that high-frequency problems need more units; no other PDE family, dimensionality or systematic scale sweep is evaluated.

Abstract: "Our experiments show that brain-inspired PINN training leads to PINN architectures that minimize the computing and memory resources yet provide accurate results" — Sec 4 shows exactly this on 1D Poisson problems with the accuracy loss disclosed ("only affected by a small loss of accuracy when compared to large fully-connected MLP"); the demonstration-only scope is stated in Sec 3.1.

Sec III-B: motif-function attributions by citation only: "FE and FbI are related to multisensory fusion [21] and enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio [20]. FI helps the network maintain a balance of excitatory and inhibitory [55]. LI plays a role in amplifying the perception of various sensory stimuli [56] and MI is linked to the rhythmic activity of neural networks [57], [58]"; no biological evidence presented.

Sec III-B/Fig 2: stated mapping from biology to architecture — "the search space ... includes local modular structure consisting of five neural motifs [FE, FI, FbI, LI, MI], and global free long-term connectivity between modules"; "We implement them with spiking neurons as shown in Fig. 2b"; modules are brain-region-inspired. The circuits are built and evolved, but no evidence bears on biological fidelity of the implementation.

Sec IV-B: component ablations with the evolutionary process held constant ("Except for the variables mentioned in the ablation experiments, the parameters and process of the evolutionary algorithm are kept constant"): motif-combination ablation ("the classification accuracy of EB-NAS is 0.88%, 1.13%, 1.18% and 2.15% higher than the best single-motif model") and connectivity ablation vs hierarchical CL-0 ("2.35%, 2.54%, 1.58% and 3.17% higher"); plus SOTA SNN comparisons (Tables III-IV) and spike-count energy comparisons.

Gains replicated across four datasets spanning static (CIFAR10, CIFAR100) and neuromorphic (CIFAR10-DVS, DVS128-Gesture) data with ablations repeated on each (Sec IV-B), but every setting is image classification; no other task family and no parameter/scale sweep of the gain is reported.

Abstract: "Extensive experiments on static datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100) and neuromorphic datasets (CIFAR10-DVS, DVS128-Gesture) demonstrate that our proposed model boosts energy efficiency, archiving consistent and remarkable performance" — Tables III-IV and the spike-count comparisons support accuracy and energy claims on exactly these datasets; the reverse claim is hedged as "preliminary insights".

Sec 1/3: the LIF neuron's computation is presented as an equation taken from the SNN literature ("behavior of classical LIF model can be modeled as follows" with membrane-potential equations, parameters tau and Vth); the paper provides no biological evidence of its own that spiking neurons perform this computation.

Sec 3: stated mapping repurposing the biological mechanism: "we incorporate the brain-inspired spiking neurons (i.e. the LIF module ...) to communicate the information between the patches in the MLP models ... We utilize LIF neuron in a full-precision manner", replacing the time axis with spatial patches (horizontal/vertical/group LIF). The module is built and ablated, but the temporal-to-spatial repurposing is a design choice, not a tested correspondence.

Sec 4.4/4.6: module-isolating ablations on the same backbone: AS-MLP-T 81.3% -> dwconv+shift 81.66% -> dwconv+LIF 81.87% (Table 5, "validates the effectiveness of both of them"); placement ablation Table 8 (Add LIF 81.38%, Sub GELU 81.21%, replace-AxialShift 81.87%); parameter ablations Table 6-7; SOTA comparisons Tables 1-4 with FLOPs reported.

Gains shown across three task families and scales: ImageNet classification (81.9%, 83.3%, 83.5% at 4.4G/8.5G/15.2G FLOPs, Table 1), COCO detection (46.0-51.4 APb, Table 2), ADE20K segmentation (Table 3), each compared against AS-MLP and Swin backbones; "all of them are higher than the base AS-MLP models" across scales (Sec 5).

Abstract: "With LIF modules, our SNN-MLP model achieves 81.9%, 83.3% and 83.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet dataset with only 4.4G, 8.5G and 15.2G FLOPs, respectively, which are state-of-the-art results as far as we know" — Tables 1-3 and the Figure 1 Pareto frontier support exactly this, with the SOTA claim scoped ("as far as we know") to MLPs.

Abstract/Sec 1: "Spiking Neural Networks transmit information through spike sequences, which encode both temporal and spatial information" ([1]); neuron models (IF, LIF, HH) listed from literature; the paper presents no biological evidence that spiking neurons perform this computation.

Sec 3: spiking Transformer blocks substitute ANN blocks in a diffusion policy ("The main difference between them is whether there is Spiking Transformer (ST)"), with a Spiking Modulate Decoder; LIF neurons with direct training and surrogate gradients, direct encoding "where the input is replicated across eight time steps". The architecture is built and run, but nothing tests biological fidelity of the instantiation.

Sec 4.2 Table 1: controlled grid over spiking (ST) and modulate-block (M-Block) factors: DPT 0.707/0.860/0.720/0.540 vs STMDP 0.754/0.940/0.800/0.540 on PushT/Can/Square/ToolHang; Table 2 ablation isolates the SMD module. Critical pattern: the spiking-only variant SDPT collapses (Can 0.220, Square 0.040, ToolHang 0.000), so the gain tracks the SMD module more than the spiking substitution itself.

Four robotic manipulation tasks (PushT, Can, Square, ToolHang) with 500-experiment averaging; all within the manipulation family; the gain does not transfer uniformly (ToolHang 0.540 equals DPT and is below DIT's 0.780; Square ties DIT at 0.800); no scale sweep or other task family.

Abstract: "Our model consistently outperforms existing Transformer-based diffusion policy method. Especially in Can task, we achieved an improvement of 8%" — but the paper's own Table 1 shows ToolHang 0.540 below the Transformer-based DIT's 0.780 and Square 0.800 only tying DIT; the 8% Can gain is measured against DPT (0.860->0.940) while DIT already reached 0.920.

Sec 1: "it leverages mechanisms such as selective neuroplasticity [7, 8], attentional modulation [9], and progressive learning [10] to rapidly adapt to new tasks while preserving overall system stability"; no specific biological structure (region, circuit, cell type) is named, and the paper presents no biological evidence of its own for any structure-computation link.

Sec 2.3.1: "we introduce Focal Loss as a brain-inspired attention modulation mechanism" (Eq 7, dynamic sample weighting); Sec 2.5: staged freezing then unfreezing of theta_high "simulates the 'locally plastic, globally stable' learning process observed in biological neural systems"; components are built and run in one setting (Sec 3), the correspondence itself is never tested.

Sec 3.4, Table 4: Brain-Inspired Hybrid 85.00%/AUC 0.9372 vs ResNet18 76.67%, ResNet34 79.17%, Quantum-Enhanced ResNet18 81.67%; "Our proposed brain-inspired hybrid model outperformed all baseline methods across all metrics".

Sec 4: "Despite the promising results achieved on the single-modality coronary angiography task, several limitations remain"; the only evaluation is binary CAG classification on one 120-image test set (Sec 3.2, Tables 1-3); no second task family, scale variation or component ablation appears anywhere.

Abstract: "strong and stable performance in binary coronary angiography classification" matches Tables 1-2, but the abstract Conclusion states "This study validates the effectiveness of brain-inspired learning mechanisms in lightweight medical image analysis and provides a biologically plausible and deployable solution".

Sec 1: "A key factor that protects humans from drastic forgetting is thought to be the reactivation of neural activity patterns representing previous experiences - referred to as memory replay (Wilson and McNaughton [1994], Rasch and Born [2007]...)"; Appendix A adds hippocampal functions (binding, spatial memory, temporary storage) from Bear et al. 2020 (p. 838, 846, Fig 24.25). All structure-computation links are carried by citation; the paper contributes no biological evidence of its own.

App B: "the early layers are considered the visual cortex, and the top layers are considered the hippocampus"; "The generator that produces the replayed data is considered the hippocampus, while the main model... is considered the cortex" (Sec 2); internal replay "replays the representations of previously learned classes at the hidden level, rather than at the input level" because "the brain doesn't replay memories down to the input level"; the model is re-implemented and run in one setting (Sec 3).

Sec 3.1: "We compare model with internal replay(w/ IR) and model without internal replay(w/o IR)... experiments both on brain-inspired replay(BIR) and... (BIR + SI)"; Fig 1: "the BIR+SI (w/ IR) model achieves the highest retention ratio and lowest forgetting score across all tasks"; Fig 2: "both w/ IR models perform worse than w/o IR models" on initial accuracy.

Sec 3.1: "We train and test on CIFAR-100 in class-IL scenario"; every analysis (Figs 1-4) is on this single dataset/scenario with 10 tasks and one architecture family; no second dataset, scenario, scale or architecture is evaluated.

Abstract: "Using the CIFAR-100 dataset in a class-incremental setting, we evaluate the effectiveness of internal replay, both in isolation and in combination with Synaptic Intelligence (SI). Our experiments show that internal replay significantly mitigates forgetting... but at the cost of reduced initial task accuracy" - exactly what Figs 1-2 show.

Intro: "converging evidence links reinforcement learning to specific neural substrates... the neuromodulator known as dopamine provides basal ganglia target structures with phasic signals that convey a reward prediction error which can influence learning and action selection" [3]; learning subsystems (neocortex, hippocampal formation, cerebellum, basal ganglia) attributed via Niv [2]. All structure-computation links are citation-only; the paper contributes no biological evidence.

Abstract: "we trained the driving agent using a brain-inspired trial-and-error technique, which was in line with the real world situation"; the artifact (modified DRQN: raw-screen input, LSTM for history, prioritized replay, weighting layer, Sec II-C/II-D) instantiates trial-and-error RL and is run on one game (Sec III); no component is mapped to a biological structure.

Sec III-D, Table I: Our model 98.33/166/213 s vs Stanford 97.46/129.09 (1 DNF)/138.37 (2 DNF) vs Human 94.07/125.30/129.50 on Farm/Raceway/Mountain; the paper concedes "our results seemed to require a longer period to finish the race" while claiming unquantified "better robustness" when the agent deviates from the driveway.

All evidence is one game (OpenAI Gym Mario Kart 64 wrapper, Sec III-A) on three tracks with a separate weight set per track (Sec III-B); no second task family, no scale study and no component ablation exists in the paper.

Abstract: "After training for several episodes, the resulting driving agent performed advanced behaviors in the given scene. We hope that in the future, the proposed brain-inspired learning system would inspire practicable self-driving control solutions" - claims stay inside the simulated setting (OpenAI Gym, Sec III).

Sec II-A: "Neuroscience has shown that the brain's hippocampal-entorhinal cortex neural circuit contains a large number of heterogeneous navigation cells. Their interactions form the basis of spatial cognition and navigation abilities [18]"; Sec II-B: "Numerous studies have confirmed that GCs located in the medial entorhinal cortex are critically important for the realization of PI capability". Structure-computation link (HDC/GC circuit performs path integration) is asserted by citation only ([2] McNaughton 2006; [18] Finkelstein 2016); the paper presents no biological evidence of its own.

Sec III-A: "This paper uses the decoded values of the CANN-modeled HDC as the training labels for the model"; Sec IV-D Figs 6-9 compare ANN-fitted decoding and bump activity against the CANN original ("the decoding effect fitted by ANNs does not deviate significantly from that of CANN, when facing several abrupt changes"). The mapping is stated and has its own side-by-side comparison (Sec IV-D, Figs 6-9).

Sec IV-B/C: parameters kept consistent with NeuroSLAM ("Parameter configurations, except those related to navigation cell modeling, were shared"), LCD excluded from timing for fairness; Table I: this work matches NeuroSLAM's MAE/RMSE/MTE (2.5/2.9/5.9 m) at 721.6 s vs 871.4 s on PC (-17.5%) and 756.1 s vs 1478.1 s on Raspberry Pi 4B (-48.9%).

Sec IV-C: "We trained two additional HDCN and GCN networks with resolutions of 25/75 and 49/147 neurons... All the three achieved identical trajectory error performance"; two datasets (parking garage 12583 frames ~600 m; self-built corridor 126.4 m) and two platforms (PC, Raspberry Pi 4B); Sec VI: "this paper has currently only explored the brain-inspired PI method itself".

Abstract: "comparable positioning accuracy to NeuroSLAM... approximately 17.5% improvement on general-purpose computing platforms and 40~50% on edge devices"; supported by Table I (accuracy 2.5/2.9/5.9 m; time cost rows) and Sec IV-C (17.5% PC; 39.4% and 48.9% on Raspberry Pi 4B); replication claim supported qualitatively by Figs 6-9.

Sec 'Processes that support learning in the brain' (p.1-2): "Plasticity of synapses specifically refers to the modification of the strength of synaptic transmission based on activity and is currently the most widely investigated mechanism by which the brain adapts to new information 17,18"; "STDP has been observed in a variety of biological systems, including the neocortex, hippocampus, and cerebellum". All structure-computation links are citation-based synthesis; the review presents no evidence of its own.

Fig 2 caption: "There are strong parallels between artificial and brain-like learning algorithms"; Fig 3 caption: "Synaptic Plasticity algorithms represent computational models that emulate the brain's ability to strengthen or weaken synapses... based on their activity, thereby facilitating learning and memory formation"; mappings stated as equations (Hebbian dw=eta*x_i*x_j; STDP piecewise exponential, p.3-4).

The review runs no own comparison; advantages are surveyed from cited work ("modelling studies have shown advantages of SNNs, such as better energy efficiency", p.3) and the review itself cautions: "These benefits are not solely attributed to their increased biological plausibility, but also to the unique properties of spiking neural networks" (p.3); "backpropagation-derived local learning rules exhibit worse and more variable generalization" than BPTT (p.7).

No own generality experiment; generality statements are second-hand: "The extent to which discovered learning rules generalize to a wide range of tasks is a significant open question" (p.9); FA "performance on larger datasets such as ImageNet is often suboptimal" (p.6); SS "capable of achieving comparable performance to backpropagation, even on large-scale datasets" (p.6).

Abstract: "This paper presents a comprehensive review of current brain-inspired learning representations in artificial neural networks... Moreover, we delve into the potential advantages and challenges accompanying this approach. Ultimately, we pinpoint promising avenues for future research". The paper delivers exactly this survey (mechanisms p.1-5; ANN learning algorithms p.5-9; applications p.9-10; conclusion p.10-11).

Sec 3: "the dual-memory model of mammalian memory (McClelland et al., 1995), which has considerable experimental support from neuroscience (Frankland et al., 2004; Takashima et al., 2006; Kitamura et al., 2017; ...)"; "Kitamura et al. (2017) performed contextual fear conditioning (CFC) experiments in mice to trace the formation and consolidation of recent memories to long-term storage... BLA... would shift where it retrieved the corresponding memory from (HC or mPFC)". The structure-computation links (HC->recent, mPFC->remote, BLA->selection, sleep->consolidation) are all established by citation; the paper presents no biological evidence of its own.

Sec 4: "FearNet's HC model is a variant of a probabilistic neural network" (Eqs 1-2); "FearNet's mPFC is implemented using a DNN trained both to reconstruct its input... and to compute P(C=k|x)" (Sec 4.1); "FearNet uses the BLA network... to determine whether to classify an input x using HC or mPFC" (Sec 4.3, Eq 5); Fig 1/Fig 3 state the mapping component-by-component. Instantiation evidence is end-to-end performance plus the BLA-vs-oracle check (Table 3); no ablation isolates the dual-memory correspondence itself.

Sec 5/6.1: comparison to FEL, GeppNet, GeppNet+STM, iCaRL, 1-NN and offline MLP on three datasets with per-model/dataset hyperparameter search ("We performed a hyperparameter search for each model/dataset combination") and shared input embeddings; Table 2: FearNet best Omega_base and Omega_all on all three datasets (mean Omega_all 0.923 vs iCaRL 0.782); Table S5 re-tests iCaRL at 100 EPC; component ablations in Tables 3, 6 and Fig 5.

Sec 6.2: base-knowledge size swept 10-150 classes (Fig S2), sleep frequency 1-15 sessions (Fig 5), multi-modal incremental learning CIFAR-100+AudioSet (Table 4), memory footprint vs 1,000 classes (Table 5, explicitly "a hypothetical extrapolation"); Sec 7: "FearNet can be adapted to other paradigms, such as unsupervised learning and regression" (untested).

Abstract: "FearNet achieves state-of-the-art performance at incremental class learning on image (CIFAR-100, CUB-200) and audio classification (AudioSet) benchmarks" and "does not store previous examples, making it memory efficient"; supported by Table 2 (best Omega_base/Omega_all on all three datasets), Table S5 (iCaRL at 100 EPC still below FearNet) and Table 5 (10.7 MB vs iCaRL 17.6 MB at 100 classes).

Sec I-A: "Biological neurons have been shown to exhibit a variety of temporally complex spiking patterns which can be summarized by various models of ordinary differential equations... [8]"; chattering attributed by citation: "As mentioned by Gray and McCormick, 'chattering cells may make a substantial intracortical contribution to the generation of synchronous cortical oscillations' [20]"; heterogeneity benefit cited via [1],[2],[9],[19]. The structure-computation links are citation-only; the paper presents no biological evidence of its own.

Sec II-A: "In combination, these four tunable bias nodes represent the parameters of the neuron's behavior" (Vth->threshold, VleakM->membrane leakage, VleakR->refractory leakage, Vp->positive feedback); per-parameter tuning verified one at a time against the standard coincidence-detection pattern (Fig 2 a-f; firing rate vs input amplitude at three Vth values, Fig 3); three patterns demonstrated: "regular spiking, fast spiking, and chattering" (Fig 5).

Sec III-B: single-layer PSNN with MZI mesh reaches "89.3% accuracy for this offline training method" on Iris (Fig 9, confusion matrix); energy "1.18 pJ/spike" from Cadence Spectre simulation (Sec III-C); Loihi comparison uses literature numbers ("Loihi shows an energetic cost of 1.7pJ/spike", Sec IV). No control attributes the gains to the heterogeneous/programmable dynamics: no homogeneous (LIF-only) neuron control on the same task, no Iris baseline comparison.

Demonstrated setting is one small task: Iris 3-class classification, 150 samples, 4 features, a single neuron and a 4x4 MZI mesh (Sec III-B, Fig 6, Fig 9); behavior generality shown only as circuit tuning regimes (Figs 2, 5); 7nm figures are ASAP7 simulations ("is predicted to achieve 36.84 fJ/spike", Abstract; Table I, Appendix Fig 1); no task family or network scale beyond the single-neuron single-layer demo is tested.

Abstract claims map to specific artifacts: four parameters tuned under 1GSpike/s -> Figs 2-3; "three spiking patterns, including chattering" -> Fig 5; PSNN "89.3% accuracy on the Iris dataset" -> Fig 9 and confusion matrix; "1.18 pJ/spike output" -> Sec III-C/Table I; "predicted to achieve 36.84 fJ/spike... with a 7 nm CMOS platform" explicitly labelled a prediction -> Table I, Appendix Fig 1.

Intro/Methods: ATTNet "is inspired by biased-competition theory" (Desimone & Duncan, 1995); "positioning of V4 between early visual and ventral... makes it a key attention control structure, which is in line with the literature showing that effects of attention are most strongly observed in this area (Bichot, Rossi, & Desimone, 2005; Chelazzi, Miller, Duncan, & Desimone, 2001)"; PPC "long believed to be responsible for the spatial prioritization of visual inputs" (Bisley & Goldberg, 2010; Ptak, 2012). Structure-computation links (V4 routing, PPC priority maps) are citation-only; no biological evidence of its own.

Methods: "The convolutional layers of this network grossly approximate visual processing in areas V1 to V4, with the output of the final convolutional layer being the V4 activation"; "ATTNet models IT processing using two trainable fully-connected layers" feeding "a prefrontal layer"; "Dorsal processing is modeled using two PPC layers"; attention modeled as a 4*4 selective routing window. Instantiation evidence is one setting: Fig 1e priority maps biased to the target category and Fig 1f guidance curves vs subjects ("while not as strong as the subjects, ATTNet shows guidance to the target").

Results: the model "learned to shift its attention to the visual features of a target category" and "ATTNet shows guidance to the target by preferentially fixating the target in earlier eye-movements" (Fig 1f), the only quantitative outcome; the abstract's utility wording ("prioritize these shifts... so as to maximize success of the ventral pathway classification and receive greater reward") reflects the RL training objective. No accuracy numbers, no baseline or ablation isolating the routing mechanism's contribution.

Single demonstrated setting only: categorical search for one target category (microwave) in 2000 COCO kitchen scenes for training and 80 disjoint test images with 30 subjects (Methods); no second task, dataset, scale variation, or ablation appears anywhere in the text.

Abstract claims map to the delivered artifacts: learned attention shifts and target guidance -> Fig 1e priority/fixation-density maps and Fig 1f guidance curves for ATTNet vs subjects; "Model behavior was tested against the fixations made by subjects" -> 30-subject comparison (Methods); the closing claim ("a step toward a better understanding") is hedged.
